subject: Architecture
title: The Internet of Buildings
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Internet of Buildings usable.

hook.text: Smart buildings have thousands of sensors monitoring everything — air quality, occupancy, even pipe pressure.

buildup.text: HVAC, lighting, elevators, and security all connect through a building management system — a brain for the structure.

discovery.text: Microsoft's Redmond campus uses 30,000 sensors. The system reduces energy waste by adjusting to real-time use.

twist.text: These systems create privacy concerns — employers can track exactly where workers sit and for how long.

climax.text: Smart buildings can cut energy use by 30-50% — critical for meeting climate targets in the built environment.

punchline.text: Your building knows you're here. It turned on the lights before you arrived.

quiz.question: How much energy can smart building systems typically save?

details.summary: The Internet of Buildings connects multiple smart buildings into networked systems that share energy, data, and resources. Buildings in a district can balance each other's energy loads, share surplus solar power, and coordinate HVAC systems to optimize efficiency across the entire neighborhood.
details.whyItMatters: Individual smart buildings are limited in what they can optimize. Networking them creates district-scale intelligence where buildings cooperate, reducing energy waste and costs beyond what any single building could achieve alone.
takeaways: Networked buildings share energy, data, and resources
District-scale systems balance loads across multiple buildings
Cooperation reduces waste beyond individual building optimization

faq.question: How do buildings share energy with each other?
faq.answer: A microgrid connects buildings so that surplus solar energy from one can power another. A building cooling down in the evening can send excess thermal energy to one heating up. Smart controllers negotiate transfers in real-time based on price signals and demand predictions.

faq.question: Is the Internet of Buildings already happening?
faq.answer: Yes, in pilot projects. University campuses, corporate parks, and new smart city districts in Singapore, Helsinki, and Toronto are implementing building-to-building energy sharing. The technology works but requires new regulatory frameworks for energy trading between buildings.
